title: Audit log pipeline operational guidance and indexing checklist
content:
Purpose and scope:
This doc collects operational guidance for our audit-log storage and retention pipeline: index mapping, practical retention windows across tiers, backfill strategy, common failure modes and mitigation, SIEM export considerations, and how RBAC v2/evidence automation affects retention decisions. It is intended for SRE, infra, security, and compliance engineers who operate the audit-log ingestion and retention pipelines.

High-level goals:
- Ensure reliable, searchable audit trail for 1) security investigations, 2) regulatory e-discovery, 3) customer evidence requests.
- Keep storage cost predictable by tiering and TTL enforcement.
- Ensure backfills and reindexing are idempotent and observable.
- Provide clear behavior on legal holds and RBAC v2-driven access gating.

Retention tiers (recommended):
- Hot (30 days): indexed, full-text, low-latency queries (Elasticsearch cluster hots). Primary for incident response and real-time alerts.
- Warm (31–365 days): compressed indices, reduced replica count, slower queries allowed. Retain full JSON but avoid frequent reindexing.
- Cold (365–1825 days / up to 5 yrs): object storage (S3), indexed metadata only (event id, timestamp, actor, action, resource, schema_version) and flattened pointers to raw blobs. Query via async archive search.
- Archive / Legal-hold: indefinite until explicit release. Stored in immutable buckets with WORM policy.

Retention enforcement rules:
- Pipeline writes a retention_tier tag at ingestion based on event_type and customer_tier. Default mapping lives in config service: /infra/configs/audit-retention-mapping.
- A compliance job runs daily to enforce TTL: moves indices or exports blobs to object store. Use manifest file per-day to drive movement (ensures idempotency).
- Legal hold flag: per-customer or per-case marker that sets retention_tier to archive and disables TTL for affected event ranges. Must be set via compliance API and audited.

Indexing and mapping notes:
- Primary search index schema should include: event_id, ts_iso, actor_id, actor_type, action, resource_type, resource_id, outcome, request_id, schema_version, ingest_host, tags, retention_tier. Keep nested objects minimal to avoid painful mapping updates.
- Use keyword fields for actor_id/resource_id, text only for reason/message.
- Versioned mappings: prefix index names with v{schema_version}-audit-YYYYMMDD. This simplifies migration/backfill.
- Disable _all; use explicit copy_to if necessary.
- For high-cardinality fields (ip_address, session_id), use hashed keyword to avoid mapping explosion; keep raw value in cold/raw blobs.

Backfill strategy and implementation checklist:
- When schema_version changes or index tuning required, prefer a reindex-from-source approach: read raw blobs (S3) with event_ts filter, transform to target mapping, write to new indices.
- Backfill job characteristics:
  - Idempotent writes: use event_id as document id.
  - Checkpointing: write progress to durable offset store (kafka offset or DynamoDB) per-shard to allow resume.
  - Batching: use time-windowed batches (e.g., 1h). Tune batch size by CPU/ES bulk tolerance.
  - Rate limiting and impact window: run heavy backfills during low-traffic windows and gradually increase throughput.
- Validation: after backfill, run QA queries (count by day, schema conformance checks, sample diffs between old and new indices).

Failure modes and mitigation (most common):
1) Bulk index response 413 / cluster OOM:
   - Immediate: pause backfill, reduce bulk size, throttle retries with exponential backoff.
   - Longer term: increase heap or move older indices to warm tier.
2) Checkpoint lost / double-process events:
   - Use idempotent document id + optimistic conflict policy. Maintain per-job checkpoint manifest in S3 to allow audit and recovery.
3) Partial backfill causing inconsistent search results:
   - Run validation after each shard. Maintain a backfill-run metadata artifact (start_ts, end_ts, batches_completed, errors_count).
4) SIEM export pipeline lag or drop (downstream outage):
   - Buffer to durable queue (Kafka topic with retention). If sink unreachable, stop acking consumer to let messages remain. Alert on lag > X (configurable).
5) Retention job accidentally deletes in-legal-hold range:
   - Safeguard: retention job must check compliance API for holds before deleting; deletion requires two-step confirmation in logs and a delete_manifest that is reversible for 72h.

Monitoring and alerts:
- Key metrics: ingestion rate (events/sec), avg indexing latency, bulk request fail rate, backfill progress percent, SIEM export lag, retention-job-deletes-per-hour, legal-hold-check-failures.
- Dashboards: per-customer retention inventory, daily index size by tier, cost burn-rate forecast for next 90 days.
- Alerts: set paged alerts for: sustained bulk failures, retention job attempting to delete >1000 events in legal-hold scope, SIEM sink down for >10m, backfill job stuck >24h.

Operational runbook (quick play):
- Ingestion spikes / cluster pressure:
  1) Identify problematic bulk by filtering ingest_host + last_bulk_id.
  2) Scale ES ingest nodes OR reduce replica / reroute older indices to warm.
  3) Temporarily throttle non-critical sources via API key-based rate limits.
- Backfill failure mid-run:
  1) Inspect last checkpoint artifact.
  2) Restart job with smaller batch size and monitoring enabled.
  3) If index conflicts appear, re-run with overwrite_on_conflict flag and validate.
- SIEM export failure:
  1) Switch sink to backup endpoint (preconfigured).
  2) Ensure Kafka topic retention holds messages; run drain tool once sink is healthy.

RBAC v2 and evidence automation interactions:
- RBAC v2 controls which teams can query hot and warm indices via proxy-layer that enforces query-level filters. Audit of RBAC changes must be logged in the audit stream and retained per policy.
- Evidence automation (customer evidence requests) will trigger an evidence job that: 1) queries indices for matching events, 2) gathers raw blobs from cold store, 3) packages results with hash-signed manifest. Evidence jobs must not bypass legal-hold checks and must create an audit entry for data export.

Cost and sizing notes (practical):
- Rough estimate: 1M events/day ~ 60GB/day raw JSON, 12GB/day indexed (hot) depending on dedupe and schema. Warm/cold ratios vary by compression.
- Keep per-customer hot retention to 30 days by default; customers needing longer should be on dedicated retention plans to avoid cross-customer cost spikes.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Define exact SLA for SIEM delivery (suggest 99.9% within 15m).
- Finalize legal-hold UI and who can authorize release.
- Decide whether to store full raw message encrypted at rest with separate KMS per-customer for customers with dedicated private deployment.

Appendix: quick checklist before running a major backfill
- [ ] Create backfill run ticket and tag relevant stakeholders (SRE, infra, security).
- [ ] Snapshot target cluster health and index state.
- [ ] Reserve low-traffic maintenance window and set throttles.
- [ ] Configure checkpoint store and test resume logic on small subset.
- [ ] Create validation queries and expected counts.
- [ ] Ensure legal-hold API is reachable and tested.
- [ ] Notify downstream SIEM and backup sink readiness.

Notes to reviewers:
This doc is intentionally pragmatic and operation-focused. Looking for feedback on concrete retention windows, legal-hold flow details, and whether to move to a per-customer S3 partitioning model for cold storage.
